title: Watched Godzilla Minus One/Minus Color recently. I feel it is more atmospheric than the colored version. Do you agree?

commenti.body:
Full disclosure, I haven't seen Godzilla Minus Color, but I have seen the original version. Nevertheless, I suspect I'd feel the same way about this as I do the B&W version of Parasite or the "black and chrome" version of Mad Max: Fury Road, in that they're cynical gimmicks designed to try and get viewers to re-engage with a film on a purely superficial level. 

In the 80s, cinephiles roasted attempts to colorize black-and-white films like Casablanca or Citizen Kane, and rightfully so. They were revisionist, and fundamentally changed the tone when iconic shots were altered in the name of trendiness. Cinematographers and directors thought out their shot compositions with black and white contrast in mind, which was undone by later revisionism.

To the extent that more modern films, shot in color and then undergoing desaturations present a B&W "alternative", I don't see how this is any different other than just being the inversion of the same problem.

i thought minus color made the visfx look flatter. there are a lot of tricks in the film to disguise its poor budget, and at least for me, the illusion, while still solid in black and white, feels less sophisticated than in color.

Your mindset is fixed to the point of looking silly. Do you also think that all Director’s Cuts are cynical gimmicks as well, given that “If it were meant to be” that way, they would have released that version from the outset?

George Miller has gone on record saying he originally intended for Mad Max: Fury Road to be in b&w. Still think it’s a cynical gimmick?

Regarding your example with director's cuts, no, I would not say that, as director's cuts generally exist because some form of studio interference or constraints were involved with the theatrical cut. A director's cut is, by most accounts, more accurate to a directorial vision that has otherwise been compromised. That doesn't necessarily mean all director's cuts are superior to the theatrical cut, but they are at least legitimate.

I totally agree.

With B&W you need more contrast. That's why they would use colored filters to shift the contrast on different color channels depending on the shot. Simply desaturating a color film leaves you with a grayscale image that is too low contrast to have the same impact as a B&W film.

Yes, but if a director intended for a movie to be b&w and supposedly filmed around that, is that not the same? 

I don't really have a horse in this race, I think I tend to agree with you, but I also don't believe most studios are going to allow a theatrical b&w experience.

I prefer the b&w version myself. To me a horror or monster film which takes place far in the past can really benefit from that extra dreamlike abstraction that the absence of color can give it - to me it actually made the film more believable in an odd way than less. It may also have to do with my respect for the 1954 original GODZILLA and how this one feels closer to it than any other I've seen. And this is also coming from someone who didn't care for MAD MAX FURY ROAD in b&w because that story feels like it needs color to make it more impactful. George Miller was very gung ho about that version but it didn't add to it for me.

I loved *Godzilla Minus One*, and being in Black and White doesn't harm it in any substantial way. I don't think the color adds overmuch to the experience, with the exception of the boat scene really benefiting from the great blue sea as a setpiece. So it's fine... but no, I don't prefer it.

Movies that are shot with the intent of being black and white can accomplish some really dramatic effects with that limitation that color loses--and of course, color has its own advantages. But this movie doesn't really use that limitation to great effect. 

I might feel a little more positive toward Minus Color if I hadn't just watched the new *Ripley* Netflix series, which uses black and white to *gorgeous* effect, such that I can't imagine that being colorized and maintaining the same punch. By comparison, Minus Color just doesn't use the effect to do any real stylistic or dramatic lifting.

As a result, it's just "good enough," and not really outstanding as an aesthetic.

I saw both versions in the theater and I can say I vastly prefer the color version.  Minus Color is a fun little Blu-ray extra, and there ARE a few brief moments that look almost like they could be from the original Godzilla, but overall you're losing some fantastic visuals from the scenes on open ocean, which are some of the most important scenes.

I'm not really sure where this black and white trend comes from.  For The Mist it made some sense considering the movie is supposed to be evocative of movies, but generally speaking, if the film wasn't shot with it being in black and white in mind, the lighting never looks as good as it should.

While I haven't seen the B&W Godzilla Minus One, based on the interviews it isn't a case where they just applied a basic grayscale filter over it - it seems like they slowly worked through the footage with the guidance of the director, presumably to ensure that the contrast was where it needed to be.

>...and supposedly filmed with that in mind

Is there evidence to support this? Presumably the studio said the film would need to be released in color before it was even shot, and if that was the case I would assume George Miller was focused on prioritizing the quality of the film he *was* shooting and not the film he *wished* he could shoot.

More to the general point though - you can't make a "director's cut" with material you never shot. While you can obviously turn a color film into a B&W film after the fact, it likely won't be the same as what the director would've created if they hadn't been pushed to make a color version.
